Zitkála-Šá worked relentlessly to gain full civil rights for Native Americans, and her efforts directly influenced the passage of the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924. In 1926, she co-founded the National Council of American Indians, serving as its president until her death in 1938. /6

Zitkála-Šá’s writing is celebrated for its lyrical intensity and its dual role as both cultural preservation and fierce political critique. She published works such as Old Indian Legends (1901) and American Indian Stories (1921), which brought Indigenous narratives to a mainstream audience. /5

The Sun Dance Opera blends European operatic structures with Indigenous melodies and rituals that were outlawed by the U.S. government. It culminates in the Sun Dance, a sacred Plains ceremony of healing, preserving the ceremony by staging it under the guise of “art and entertainment.” /4

Despite these challenges, Zitkála-Šá excelled academically, later attending Earlham College and the New England Conservatory of Music. A talented violinist, she co-composed The Sun Dance Opera (1913), the first opera written by a Native American woman and a unique form of cultural resistance. /3
